title: A Zoom Screen-Sharing Bug Let Anyone Take Over Other Devices on a Call
gist: Digital defense firm A Security used publicly available AI models and fewer than 20 prompts to find Zoom screen-sharing annotation vulnerabilities that allowed silent, zero-interaction device takeover of any participant or host across every OS Zoom supports. The economic point is the collapse in cost: work the researchers estimate would have taken five people six months now takes under 20 prompts, making AI-enabled vulnerability discovery a democratized capability.

insights.claim: Researchers at A Security discovered the Zoom vulnerabilities in early June using publicly available AI models, and it took fewer than 20 prompts to uncover the flaws and build a working attack.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Off-the-shelf commercial models — not bespoke tooling — are now sufficient for enterprise-grade exploit development, which resets threat models for every software vendor.
insights.locator: Researchers from the digital defense firm A Security

insights.claim: A Security's cofounder estimates the same discovery would previously have taken a team of five people roughly six months of refining and iteration, versus under 20 prompts today — roughly a two-to-three-order-of-magnitude cost collapse in offensive research.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: If exploit-discovery cost falls by orders of magnitude, expected vulnerability disclosure volume and patch cadence must rise — structurally bullish for security spend and bearish for legacy proprietary codebases.
insights.quote: Before it would have taken a team of five people maybe six months with a lot of refining and iteration to find this. Now people can reach the same results with under 20 prompts.
insights.locator: What is interesting for us and what we believe is dangerous

insights.claim: The named danger is democratization rather than capability — the barrier to entry for finding and weaponizing software flaws is dropping rapidly.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Threat actor population widens far beyond nation-states and organized crime, raising baseline breach frequency across the mid-market.
insights.quote: What is interesting for us and what we believe is dangerous is the democratization of these capabilities—the barrier to entry is dropping rapidly,

insights.claim: Security's traditional 'cat-and-mouse game' framing is being replaced by an all-out race as AI bug hunting proliferates.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Defensive teams that cannot match attacker iteration speed lose by default — favors vendors selling automated patching and continuous testing over periodic audit models.
insights.quote: as AI bug hunting proliferates, this delicate dance has become an all-out race

themes.theme: Where AI hunts: obscure code in closed source

insights.claim: The AI bug hunting systems deliberately targeted Zoom's real-time annotation protocol used during screen sharing because, like human bug hunters, they are trained that convoluted and obscure functions often contain overlooked vulnerabilities.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Reusable audit heuristic: esoteric, rarely-exercised features are the highest-yield attack surface — worth prioritizing in any software due diligence.
insights.locator: The vulnerabilities were specifically in the protocol

insights.claim: Proprietary closed-source software is argued to be more exposed because complex but esoteric features like annotation never get the benefit of public open review, even when the vendor does extensive internal code review.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: A structural argument that closed-source SaaS carries higher latent vulnerability density — relevant when comparing security risk across enterprise software vendors.
insights.quote: without the benefit of public, open review, esoteric yet complex features like annotation are more likely to contain mistakes
insights.locator: This is particularly true with proprietary, closed-source software

themes.theme: Blast radius and enterprise lateral movement

insights.claim: Anyone on a Zoom call involving screen sharing, whether participant or host, was vulnerable to a silent attack carried out with no indication and no interaction from the victim.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Zero-click, zero-indication exploitation on a universally deployed collaboration tool is close to worst-case for enterprise exposure assessment.
insights.locator: Anyone on a call that involved screen sharing

insights.claim: The flaws affected devices running every operating system Zoom supports — Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS and Android — and required both server-side and client-side fixes.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Cross-platform protocol-level bugs cannot be mitigated by endpoint diversity, and dual-side patching means slower real-world remediation.
insights.locator: Zoom issued a security advisory on Tuesday

insights.claim: The researchers describe the worst case as taking over an entire enterprise from a single call: control a company employee's computer and credentials, then move laterally through the organization.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Converts a video-conferencing bug into full enterprise-compromise risk — the kind of vector that drives cyber-insurance repricing and zero-trust budget approvals.
insights.quote: If you just get on a Zoom with us, we can take over your device,
insights.locator: A Security cofounder Yossi Torati told WIRED

insights.claim: Zoom is called an especially valuable target because joining a call is itself a gesture of trust and the platform is widely used for events and semipublic activities like webinars, so users have their guard down.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Trust-by-default collaboration tools are the highest-leverage targets; expect security controls and vendor scrutiny to shift toward this category.
insights.quote: And Zoom is an important type of target because people assume trust when using it. They don’t see it as a threat.
insights.locator: Before it would have taken a team of five people

insights.claim: Zoom issued a security advisory and began rolling out fixes but did not respond to multiple requests for comment from WIRED about the A Security findings.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Silence on a zero-click enterprise takeover disclosure is a communications-risk signal worth tracking alongside the technical remediation.
insights.locator: Zoom did not respond to multiple requests for comment
